geography: New York City, USA; authority and outcome footprint vary by case
interpretation: Evidence atlas, not a city Doughnut score or additive causal model. Native units remain separate. Slice mapping is conceptual; no estimate establishes a sufficiency-threshold crossing, ecological restoration, or joint household wellbeing.

policies.title: Universal free school meals
policies.jurisdiction: NYC public schools; federal reimbursement framework
policies.status: Implemented citywide September 7, 2017; evaluated earlier school-level provision, NOT the 2017 citywide expansion
policies.mechanism: Remove lunch prices and means-testing stigma; increase meal participation and learning readiness.

headline.label: Lunch participation increase, poor middle-school students

outcomes.counterfactual: Within-student changes in UFM exposure with grade-by-year controls; non-UFM experience

reference_participation_rates.note: Paper comparison means, not randomized untreated baselines

policies.observed_outcomes: 2017 official rollout expanded free-lunch eligibility from 75% to all public-school students; this is coverage, not measured food-security improvement.
policies.design: Longitudinal difference-in-differences with student fixed effects; participation sample 47,887 students and 122,685 student-years. Test-score sample: 222,456 students / 659,797 observations, same 2010–2013 window; not the smaller participation sample.
policies.distribution: Both income groups gain; larger participation/test estimates for students not previously classified poor.
policies.costs_tradeoffs: Federal CEP reimbursement shifted financing; meal production still consumes resources. Added consumption, food waste and supply-chain footprints were not estimated here.
policies.limitations: Historical middle-school estimates are not the citywide 2017 treatment effect. Weight effects mostly statistically insignificant; no evidence of obesity increase is not proof of nutritional sufficiency. School selection and changing exposure require identifying assumptions. Breakfast participation null; non-poor attendance -0.124pp (p<.10), approximately one-fifth school day; other attendance effects insignificant.

policies.title: Tenant Right to Counsel / Universal Access
policies.jurisdiction: NYC Office of Civil Justice contracts; proceedings in New York State Housing Court
policies.status: Local Law 136 (2017); expanded citywide, with substantial representation gaps
policies.mechanism: Publicly funded counsel changes legal defense and bargaining for tenants at or below 200% federal poverty guidelines.

headline.label: Eviction probability across cases: program rollout reduced-form estimate

outcomes.estimand: Program introduction across all housing-court cases in targeted ZIP codes
IV local effect of representation among tenants induced to obtain counsel

policies.observed_outcomes: Comptroller (May 2025): representation fell from 71% in Q4 FY2021 to 42% in Q4 FY2024; Bronx 81% to 31%. FY2024 represented-household retention of 89% is selected-service descriptive data, NOT 89% evictions prevented.
policies.design: ZIP rollout instruments counsel; ZIP and borough-by-month fixed effects, detailed case covariates; 727,692 cases.
policies.counterfactual: Same ZIP before rollout, net contemporaneous borough changes and covariates; IV requires exclusion/monotonicity.
policies.distribution: Larger estimated gains for high-risk tenants; service gaps concentrated in Bronx and low-income Black/Latine communities.
policies.costs_tradeoffs: Counsel is a real staffing/fiscal cost. Longer adjudication benefits tenants but delays landlords: +85 days to judgment in primary IV specification. 2023 RFx contemplated $408m over FY2025–27, not verified expenditure.
policies.limitations: Address-fixed-effect eviction estimate -5.8pp (SE 3.4) is less precise. No long-run rent/supply conclusion; no measured homelessness effect. Early rollout estimates cannot establish current program effectiveness.

sources.title: Cassidy & Currie (2023), The effects of legal representation on tenant outcomes in housing court, Journal of Public Economics 222:104844

policies.title: Clean Heat: phase out No. 6 heating oil
policies.jurisdiction: NYC DEP regulation with NYC assistance; related NY State sulfur standards
policies.status: 2011 rule; assistance 2012; No. 6 deadline June 30, 2015; converted buildings assessed through 2016
policies.mechanism: Replace dirty residual heating oil with cleaner fuels; reduce local combustion pollution. Distinct from LL97 and the later NYS heat-pump incentive program.

headline.unit: μg/m³ PM2.5 per 10 converted buildings per census tract
headline.label: Adjusted pollution association

outcomes.unit: μg/m³ per 10 converted buildings per tract
ppb per 10 converted buildings per tract
ppb per 10 converted buildings per tract

policies.observed_outcomes: City reports more than 5,300 registered No. 6 buildings converted during 2012–2015. Avoided deaths quoted by officials are MODELED, not counted mortality effects.
policies.design: Spatial-lag regression across 2,151 tracts; modeled NYCCAS exposure surfaces and fuel-conversion records; controls include traffic, fuel shifts, income and building age.
policies.counterfactual: Conditional relationship between conversion intensity and pollution change; not randomized or untreated-city difference-in-differences.
policies.distribution: Poorer buildings could switch to intermediate No. 4 rather than cleanest alternatives; financing and information barriers matter.
policies.costs_tradeoffs: Boiler conversions require capital. Gas substitution can improve local pollutants without establishing life-cycle climate gains; methane/leakage not quantified here.
policies.limitations: Separate 48-apartment study found indoor PM2.5 unchanged at 12.8 μg/m³ (p=.99). Raw outdoor PM2.5 fell 8.96→8.08 (p=.08); reference-site-corrected outdoor reduction was significant (p=.04, Table 6). No systematic cleaner-fuel versus No. 4 differences were observed. Ambient associations do not prove personal exposure or health improvements; conversion coefficient is not the citywide policy effect.

policies.title: Congestion Relief Zone tolling
policies.jurisdiction: MTA Bridges and Tunnels / New York State; NYC and NYSDOT project partners
policies.status: Operating since January 5, 2025; evidence reviewed through October 26, 2026
policies.mechanism: Price road congestion; change trips/routes/timing and fund transit. Faster roads are not themselves proof of equitable access or lower emissions.

headline.label: Cordon-area speed increase vs synthetic counterfactual

outcomes.counterfactual: Generalized synthetic control using granular Google Maps data

outcomes.sensitivity: Spillover-adjusted -1.33 μg/m³; nearby non-CRZ +0.50 μg/m³, p=.34; satellite NO2 attributable -1.23%, p=.096

policies.observed_outcomes: Official NYC Health full-year 2025 vs 2024 evaluation found no statistically significant policy-attributable pollution difference within CRZ. EJ sites showed no attributable increase overall; BQE pollutant improvement lagged control at one site.
policies.design: Speed: generalized synthetic control. Air: predictive counterfactual at 42 monitors versus official integrated-monitor controlled evaluation; these are distinct endpoints/designs.
policies.distribution: Drivers pay; transit riders can benefit from funding. Low-income frequent-driver discount and disability exemptions mitigate but do not remove burdens; unpriced regional drivers may gain time.
policies.costs_tradeoffs: Launch peak E-ZPass car toll $9; overnight $2.25. Toll is a transfer, collection and behavioral costs are resource costs. Diversion risk requires EJ monitoring, not assumed uniform gains.
policies.limitations: Working-paper speed result; headline window must not imply all of 2026. Air estimates disagree and daily maximum differs from neighborhood-average exposure. Do not merge traffic-emissions models with ambient measurements or infer avoided deaths. Cook et al. also find little effect on consumer spending or foot traffic. October 2026 Goldberg et al. real-time-monitor DiD also reports PM2.5 benefits; primary abstract reviewed, full paper not accessed. Its satellite NO2 result is not significant at 5% despite a large regional before-after decline.

policies.title: Paid sick leave mandate
policies.jurisdiction: NYC employer mandate; later overlapping NY State law
policies.status: 2014 mandate implemented; current rules expanded since study and must not be conflated with evaluated treatment
policies.mechanism: Paid time away from work lowers income/time barriers to seeking care and staying home when ill.

headline.label: Annual probability of emergency care among continuously enrolled adult Medicaid beneficiaries

outcomes.counterfactual: Entropy-balanced Medicaid adults elsewhere in NY State

policies.observed_outcomes: Study cohort: 552,857 continuously enrolled adults age 18–64, including 361,208 NYC residents; not a sample of confirmed employed recipients.
policies.design: Difference-in-differences with individual fixed effects and entropy weights; event study and sensitivity checks.
policies.distribution: Relevant to low-income workers and carers; employment/actual leave receipt unobserved. Not all Medicaid residents were treated.
policies.costs_tradeoffs: Employers finance paid absences and coverage; reduced contagion is plausible spillover, not measured by this evaluation. NYC-specific net fiscal or employment effect not established here.
policies.limitations: ED association loses significance in traditional unweighted DiD; primary-care result loses significance with linear trends. Breast/cervical screening null. Later state mandate is outside evaluation. Do not describe -0.6pp as -0.6% or extrapolate to all city residents.
